passage:
You want to fix the whole world by Friday, Gargi. I know that look. I had it at twenty.
In my final year, your Shankar Mama ran the flood relief drive at college. I slept four hours a night, answered every phone call, and cried in the bus when a donor backed out. My roommate Pritam would leave a plate of rice on my desk, and I wouldn't touch it.
Then, in the middle of a meeting, I snapped at the one girl who was helping most. She walked out.
That night Pritam said, "You care like a flood yourself. A flood destroys too." It stung. After that, I kept Sunday mornings for sleep and cricket, and I waited till I was calm before hard talks.
We kept the drive going for two more years. So care deeply, beta. Just eat the rice.

qa.q: Who left a plate of rice on Shankar Mama's desk?
qa.a: His roommate Pritam would leave a plate of rice on his desk.

qa.q: How was young Shankar feeling during the relief drive?
qa.a: He was overwhelmed and exhausted; he slept four hours a night, cried in the bus and snapped at the helper he relied on most.

qa.q: What turning point in the story let Shankar keep caring without collapsing?
qa.a: After Pritam's words, he kept Sunday mornings for rest and waited until he was calm before hard talks, so the drive lasted two more years.

qa.q: How might Pritam have seen his roommate in those weeks?
qa.a: Pritam seems worried and caring; he quietly brought food and later told Shankar the honest thing he needed to hear.

grounding: Shankar Mama tells Gargi how his intense caring at twenty exhausted him until routines and better timing for hard talks let him keep his depth.

passage:
At the temple fair in Sonpur, little Jahnavi dropped her sugar candy in the dust and burst into tears.
Ritu, five, looked at her friend's face. Her own lip began to shake, and soon she was crying too, even louder.
Then Ritu held out her clay horse, the one she had begged Amma for. "Take it. Stop crying."
Jahnavi hugged the horse and her sobs slowed. But Ritu kept crying.
Amma bent down and wiped Ritu's cheeks. "Look, Jahnavi is smiling now. She was sad, and you were kind. You can be happy again." Ritu blinked, looked at Jahnavi, and slowly smiled back.

qa.q: What did Ritu give Jahnavi?
qa.a: Ritu held out her clay horse, the one she had begged Amma for.

qa.q: Why did Ritu start crying too?
qa.a: Seeing Jahnavi cry made Ritu feel sad as well, as if her friend's upset had become her own.

qa.q: How did Amma help Ritu, and what could other adults learn from it?
qa.a: Amma pointed out that Jahnavi was fine now and named Ritu's kindness, gently helping Ritu see her feelings were separate from her friend's.

qa.q: What is it like for Jahnavi when Ritu hands her the horse?
qa.a: She probably feels comforted and cared for, because her friend gave up something precious to cheer her up.

grounding: Ritu cries when her friend cries and offers a toy to comfort her, still learning her feelings are separate from her friend's.

passage:
Tuesday
Dear diary, today Mehak was really upset in art class because Ma'am put her painting on the board second, not first. I didn't get it. Second is still on the board! I would be happy.
But she was quiet all through lunch and didn't eat her paratha. So I asked her, "What happened?" like Mumma asks me.
She said her painting was of her Nani's house, and Nani passed away in the summer, so she wanted everyone to see it first.
Oh. So it wasn't about first and second at all. I told her it was the best house on the board and asked if she wanted to tell me about Nani. She talked for the whole break.
I still don't feel the way she does, but I think I understand now.
Akash

qa.q: Where did Ma'am put Mehak's painting?
qa.a: Ma'am put her painting on the board second, not first.

qa.q: What did Akash first think about Mehak being upset?
qa.a: Akash felt puzzled, because being second would have made Akash happy, so the upset didn't make sense at first.

qa.q: What did Akash try that could help other children understand a friend?
qa.a: Asking "What happened?" before judging, just as Mumma does, let Mehak explain the real reason and let Akash offer comfort.

qa.q: What would change for Mehak if nobody had asked her?
qa.a: She might have kept feeling sad and alone about her Nani, and her quiet lunch could have been mistaken for sulking over a place on the board.

grounding: Akash begins to understand why a friend is upset despite not feeling the same, asks what happened and helps, modelled on an adult.

passage:
At break in the school library, Neel told his classmates that his dog had died the night before.
Uday's eyes filled at once. His throat tightened so much he couldn't say a word, and he stared at the table, wishing he knew what to do.
Shankar nodded. "That's rough. Grief takes a while, right? Did you get to say bye?" Then he opened his chemistry book again.
Later, in the peer-support club, Ms Fernandes asked them both about it. "I felt it like it was my own dog," Uday said. "But I was useless."
"I knew what he was going through," Shankar admitted. "I just didn't feel much."
Ms Fernandes smiled. "Two halves of one skill. Uday, try saying one simple sentence. Shankar, try staying with him a minute longer." They agreed to practise at the next club meeting.

qa.q: What did Neel tell his classmates at break?
qa.a: He told them that his dog had died the night before.

qa.q: What was Uday feeling when Neel shared the news?
qa.a: Uday felt Neel's pain deeply, with tears and a tight throat, but also felt helpless because he didn't know what to do.

qa.q: What small step did Ms Fernandes suggest to each of them?
qa.a: She asked Uday to try one simple sentence and Shankar to stay with Neel a minute longer, so each could build the half of empathy that was missing.

qa.q: How might Neel have seen Shankar going back to his chemistry book?
qa.a: Neel may have felt a little brushed off, even though Shankar's words showed real understanding.

grounding: Uday feels his classmate's pain but freezes while Shankar understands but stays detached, and a teacher shows both can practise their skills.

passage:
First week of term. Vikas's hostel door was always open. He fixed Ramesh's laptop, lent notes to three people and stayed up till two listening to Usha cry about her breakup, then wrote half her lab report so she'd have one less worry.
Three weeks later. Vikas fell asleep in his own lab exam. When Usha texted "can u talk?? 😢" that night, he stared at the screen feeling tired and oddly angry, and didn't reply.
Next Saturday. He called Usha in daylight. "I care about you. I can listen for a bit, but I can't do your reports, and I think the hostel counsellor could help with the heavy stuff." She was quiet, then said, "Fair." They talked for twenty minutes. That night Vikas slept eight hours.

qa.q: What happened to Vikas three weeks later?
qa.a: He fell asleep in his own lab exam.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel when Usha texted that night?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and resentful, staring at the screen feeling tired and oddly angry, and he didn't reply.

qa.q: Which change made Vikas's helping sustainable?
qa.a: He kept caring and listening but stopped rescuing by doing her work, and pointed her to the hostel counsellor for the heavy problems.

qa.q: How might Usha feel when Vikas sets his limit?
qa.a: She might feel a little stung at first, then respected and supported, since he still listens and shows her where more help is.

grounding: Vikas absorbs everyone's problems until he is exhausted and resentful, then learns to care with limits and separate compassion from rescuing.

passage:
"Harsha, please. Just draft the client report tonight. I'm drowning," Farida said, leaning on his desk.
"You really are. You've had the audit, the new hire and your mum's surgery, all in one month."
"So you'll do it?"
"No. I can't write your report again."
Her face fell. "Wow. I thought you were on my side."
"I am. That's why I'm saying no. Last time you felt worse when the manager asked you questions about it."
Farida sat down heavily. "That was awful."
"Here's what I can do. I'll sit with you from six to seven and we'll outline it together. And tomorrow you could ask the manager for two extra days."
She was quiet, then gave a small, tired laugh. "You're annoying when you're right."
"I know. Get your laptop."

qa.q: What did Farida ask Harsha to do tonight?
qa.a: She asked him to draft the client report tonight.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when Harsha said no?
qa.a: She felt hurt and let down at first, saying she thought he was on her side, then tired and reluctantly relieved.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who wants to support a stressed friend without rescuing them?
qa.a: Name what they are going through, refuse the thing that would harm them, and offer a clear, limited kind of help like Harsha's hour together.

qa.q: What would change if Harsha had simply written the report?
qa.a: Farida would feel rescued tonight but might face another awful meeting and depend on him again, and Harsha could start to feel used.

grounding: Harsha understands Farida's stress without writing her report for her, showing empathy beside a firm boundary.

passage:
At dinner in their Pune flat, Tauji announced that Ganga would switch to the school near his office next year. Ganga looked at her plate and said, "Ji, Tauji." Her Dadi, calm as always, passed the dal and said, "We'll discuss it after the exams." Ganga watched how everyone went quiet for Dadi and wished she could be like her one day.
The next evening in the colony park, Ganga climbed onto the slide and argued with Nitin for twenty minutes about why girls should get more turns on the cricket pitch. She waved her arms and even stamped her foot.
"You're so loud outside," Nitin laughed. "At your house you're like a mouse."
Ganga shrugged. "At home, Tauji talks first. Here, I do." Then she jumped down and grabbed the bat.

qa.q: What did Ganga argue about with Nitin in the colony park?
qa.a: She argued about why girls should get more turns on the cricket pitch.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel as she watched Dadi at dinner?
qa.a: She felt admiration for Dadi, who stayed calm and could make everyone go quiet, and wished she could be like her one day.

qa.q: What might help Ganga feel comfortable in both places?
qa.a: Knowing that being modest at home and bold with friends are both real parts of her; later, a trusted adult like Dadi could give her space to share her view at home.

qa.q: How does Nitin see Ganga?
qa.a: Nitin finds her loud and funny outside and is surprised she is so quiet at home, like a different person in each room.

grounding: Ganga holds back her opinions with elders at home out of respect but voices them freely with a friend, showing personality differently in different rooms.

passage:
The rain had flooded the road outside the school, and the buses were an hour late. Raghav and Ira waited in the empty staff room with Mrs Bose, the debate coach.
Raghav's grandfather had died on Sunday. When Mrs Bose asked how he was, Raghav said, "Fine, ma'am. Boys don't make a fuss." His jaw was clenched.
Ira had the form for school captain folded in her bag. She hadn't filled it in. "My aunt says girls who push too much look proud," she mumbled.
Mrs Bose put down her tea. "In this room, crying is allowed, Raghav. And Ira, wanting to lead isn't pride."
Raghav's eyes filled, and for once he didn't wipe them away. Ira pulled out the form. By the time the bus horn sounded through the rain, her name was on it.

qa.q: Why were Raghav and Ira waiting in the staff room?
qa.a: The rain had flooded the road outside the school, and the buses were an hour late.

qa.q: What did Raghav's clenched jaw suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggested he was holding back deep sadness about his grandfather because he believed boys shouldn't make a fuss.

qa.q: What did Mrs Bose do that could help other teenagers?
qa.a: She gave clear permission for both a boy's tears and a girl's ambition, widening what each of them felt safe to show.

qa.q: How might Ira see Raghav crying in front of her?
qa.a: She may feel moved and trusted, and it might make her braver about showing her own hidden wish to lead.

grounding: Raghav hides sadness and Ira hides ambition because of learned gender rules, until an adult widens the range of what they may show.

passage:
The bus strike began on the same morning as Abbu's clinic appointment and the last day for Kiran's college exam form. Irfan, the eldest, woke at five.
He wheeled Abbu to the auto stand, argued the fare down, sat through the long wait, and got Abbu home by eleven. Then he rode pillion with a neighbour to Kiran's college, stood in line and submitted her form ten minutes before the counter shut.
On the way back, his phone buzzed: his friends' photos from the hill trip he had said no to. He looked for a long time.
At home Ammi asked, "All done?" Irfan said, "All done," and smiled.
Only Kiran saw him lie down on the floor mat without taking off his shoes. She brought him tea. "Bhaiya, next time, give me one of the jobs."

qa.q: How long before the counter shut did Irfan submit Kiran's form?
qa.a: He submitted her form ten minutes before the counter shut.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as he looked at his friends' trip photos?
qa.a: He felt wistful and tired, quietly wishing for the freedom he had given up to look after the family.

qa.q: What small step could help Irfan carry his duty with less strain?
qa.a: He could accept Kiran's offer and share some of the jobs, instead of hiding his tiredness behind "All done".

qa.q: How does Kiran see her brother that evening?
qa.a: She notices what the others miss, sees how worn out he is, and wants to help carry the load.

grounding: Irfan, the eldest, serves his parents and sister through a hard day, and his duty hides tiredness and a wish for freedom.

passage:
August. In his village near Hassan, Harish led the Ganesha procession, shouting jokes in the local dialect and teasing his uncles. Everyone called him the loud one.
October. In his Bengaluru college, Harish sat at the back, speaking careful English, laughing a second late at jokes. When Urmila asked where he was from, he said "near Hassan" and changed the subject. That night he felt like two people sharing one body.
December. In the canteen, Urmila told him she spoke three different ways at home, at college and at her grandmother's. "It's like switching gears," she said. Harish laughed. When a senior asked what his father did, he said clearly, "He's a farmer. Coconut and ragi." Then he told a joke from the village, in English. Half the table laughed.

qa.q: What did Harish say his father grows?
qa.a: He said his father is a farmer who grows coconut and ragi.

qa.q: How did Harish feel in October after Urmila's question?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and split, like two people sharing one body, and shy about showing where he came from.

qa.q: What helped Harish stay flexible without losing himself?
qa.a: Hearing that Urmila also switches styles let him see switching as normal, and answering honestly about his father kept his core the same.

qa.q: How might Urmila see Harish in December?
qa.a: She probably finds him warmer and more open, and feels glad her own story helped him relax.

grounding: Harish shifts style, language and boldness between his village and city college, and learns flexibility is a strength while staying honest.
